claim: Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules are dynamic condensates enriched in regulatory RNA binding proteins (RBPs) and RNAs under tight spatiotemporal control.
source: Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules are dynamic condensates enriched in regulatory RNA binding proteins (RBPs) and RNAs under tight spatiotemporal control.
evidence: This is a general characterization statement presented in the abstract, drawing from established scientific knowledge about RNP granules.

claim: RNP granules form through the self-association of RNP components into dynamic networks of interactions.
source: Extensive recent work has investigated the molecular principles underlying RNP granule assembly, unraveling that they form through the self-association of RNP components into dynamic networks of interactions.
evidence: This statement references extensive recent work, indicating it is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tyramine induces a reversible remodeling of somatic RNP granules in Drosophila brains.
source: Here, we demonstrate through high-resolution imaging of intact Drosophila brains that Tyramine induces a reversible remodeling of somatic RNP granules characterized by the decondensation of granule-enriched RBPs (e.g. Imp/ZBP1/IGF2BP) and helicases (e.g. Me31B/DDX-6/Rck).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tyramine-induced RNP granule remodeling is characterized by the decondensation of Imp/ZBP1/IGF2BP.
source: Here, we demonstrate through high-resolution imaging of intact Drosophila brains that Tyramine induces a reversible remodeling of somatic RNP granules characterized by the decondensation of granule-enriched RBPs (e.g. Imp/ZBP1/IGF2BP) and helicases (e.g. Me31B/DDX-6/Rck).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: Tyramine-induced RNP granule remodeling is characterized by the decondensation of Me31B/DDX-6/Rck.
source: Here, we demonstrate through high-resolution imaging of intact Drosophila brains that Tyramine induces a reversible remodeling of somatic RNP granules characterized by the decondensation of granule-enriched RBPs (e.g. Imp/ZBP1/IGF2BP) and helicases (e.g. Me31B/DDX-6/Rck).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: Tyramine signals through the TyrR receptor to trigger RNP component decondensation.
source: Furthermore, our functional analysis reveals that Tyramine signals both through its receptor TyrR and through the calcium-activated kinase CamkII to trigger RNP component decondensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data presented in the manuscript, including experiments with TyrR mutants.

claim: Tyramine signals through the calcium-activated kinase CamkII to trigger RNP component decondensation.
source: Furthermore, our functional analysis reveals that Tyramine signals both through its receptor TyrR and through the calcium-activated kinase CamkII to trigger RNP component decondensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis data, including experiments with CamkII inhibition.

claim: RNP granule remodeling is accompanied by the rapid and specific translational activation of associated mRNAs.
source: Finally, we uncover that RNP granule remodeling is accompanied by the rapid and specific translational activation of associated mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from translation reporter experiments and SunTag imaging.

claim: 100-200 nm-sized cytoplasmic RNP granules are visible in the cell bodies of MB γ neurons in resting brains of 10–15-day-old flies.
source: In resting brains of 10–15-day-old flies, 100-200 nm-sized cytoplasmic RNP granules are visible in the cell bodies of MB γ neurons (Figure 1A–A'' and C), a population of neurons known for its role in learning and memory (Keene and Waddell, 2007; Keleman et al., 2007; Akalal et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1 and references to prior work on MB neurons.

claim: MB γ neurons are a population of neurons known for their role in learning and memory.
source: In resting brains of 10–15-day-old flies, 100-200 nm-sized cytoplasmic RNP granules are visible in the cell bodies of MB γ neurons (Figure 1A–A'' and C), a population of neurons known for its role in learning and memory (Keene and Waddell, 2007; Keleman et al., 2007; Akalal et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on MB neurons.

claim: RNP granules in MB γ neurons contain RNAs such as profilin.
source: These granules contain RNAs such as profilin, as well as regulatory proteins that dynamically shuttle between the granular and soluble pools (Vijayakumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RNP granules in MB γ neurons contain regulatory proteins that dynamically shuttle between the granular and soluble pools.
source: These granules contain RNAs such as profilin, as well as regulatory proteins that dynamically shuttle between the granular and soluble pools (Vijayakumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The RBP Imp is among the regulatory proteins that dynamically shuttle between the granular and soluble pools in MB γ neurons.
source: Among those are the RBP Imp and the DEAD box helicase Me31B, two conserved repressors of translation (Figure 1A–A''; Minshall et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 2001; Hüttelmaier et al., 2005; Hillebrand et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and citations to prior work.

claim: The DEAD box helicase Me31B is among the regulatory proteins that dynamically shuttle between the granular and soluble pools in MB γ neurons.
source: Among those are the RBP Imp and the DEAD box helicase Me31B, two conserved repressors of translation (Figure 1A–A''; Minshall et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 2001; Hüttelmaier et al., 2005; Hillebrand et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and citations to prior work.

claim: Imp and Me31B are conserved repressors of translation.
source: Among those are the RBP Imp and the DEAD box helicase Me31B, two conserved repressors of translation (Figure 1A–A''; Minshall et al., 2001; Nakamura et al., 2001; Hüttelmaier et al., 2005; Hillebrand et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tyramine triggered the strongest response among tested neurotransmitters and neuromodulators, characterized by the decondensation of Imp molecules and a significant decrease in the number of Imp-containing granules.
source: Tyramine, a bioamine found in trace amounts in both invertebrate and mammalian brains (Burchett and Hicks, 2006; Lange, 2009), triggered the strongest response, characterized by the decondensation of Imp molecules and a significant decrease in the number of Imp-containing granules (Figure 1B,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tyramine is a bioamine found in trace amounts in both invertebrate and mammalian brains.
source: Tyramine, a bioamine found in trace amounts in both invertebrate and mammalian brains (Burchett and Hicks, 2006; Lange, 2009), triggered the strongest response, characterized by the decondensation of Imp molecules and a significant decrease in the number of Imp-containing granules (Figure 1B,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Decondensation of Imp was accompanied by a significant, although less pronounced, relocalization of Me31B protein from the granular to the cytoplasmic pool.
source: Decondensation of Imp was accompanied by a significant, although less pronounced, relocalization of Me31B protein from the granular to the cytoplasmic pool (Figure 1B').
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The relocalization of Me31B did not impact on the number of Me31B-positive granules.
source: This relocalization did not impact on the number of Me31B-positive granules (Figure 1E), but translated into a decrease in the ratio between the granular and the cytoplasmic soluble pool of Me31B (partition coefficient; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Tyramine-induced relocalization of Me31B translated into a decrease in the ratio between the granular and the cytoplasmic soluble pool of Me31B (partition coefficient).
source: This relocalization did not impact on the number of Me31B-positive granules (Figure 1E), but translated into a decrease in the ratio between the granular and the cytoplasmic soluble pool of Me31B (partition coefficient; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The re-localization of Imp and Me31B observed in the presence of Tyramine did not result from changes in protein levels.
source: Importantly, the re-localization of Imp and Me31B observed in the presence of Tyramine did not result from changes in protein levels, as similar levels of Imp and Me31B were observed with and without Tyramine treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tyramine reversibly alters the phase behavior of RNP granule components.
source: This thus suggests that Tyramine reversibly alters the phase behavior of RNP granule components.
evidence: This claim is based on recovery experiments showing that granule numbers return to baseline after Tyramine removal.

claim: After 60 min of recovery following Tyramine treatment, bright Imp-positive granules were again visible and their number returned to baseline.
source: While a significant decrease in the number of Imp-positive granules was observed after Tyramine treatment, bright Imp-positive granules were again visible after the recovery period and their number returned to baseline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by recovery experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The decreased partitioning of Me31B into granules was reverted after recovery from Tyramine treatment.
source: Similarly, the decreased partitioning of Me31B into granules was reverted after recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by recovery experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Me31B-GFP-positive granules exhibit a dynamic behavior characterized by successions of short movements and pauses, as well as both fusion and fission events.
source: This first revealed that granules exhibit a dynamic behavior characterized by successions of short movements and pauses, as well as both fusion and fission events (Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by real-time imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Relocalization of Me31B from the granular to the cytoplasm pool is initiated within minutes after Tyramine treatment.
source: This revealed that relocalization of Me31B from the granular to the cytoplasm pool is initiated within minutes after Tyramine treatment, but is a progressive rather than abrupt process.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Relocalization of Me31B from the granular to the cytoplasm pool is a progressive rather than abrupt process.
source: This revealed that relocalization of Me31B from the granular to the cytoplasm pool is initiated within minutes after Tyramine treatment, but is a progressive rather than abrupt process.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A similar trend of progressive decondensation was observed for GFP-Imp.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, a similar trend was observed for GFP-Imp, illustrated by a progressive decrease in the number of GFP-Imp-positive granules.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TyrR is a GPCR that responds specifically to Tyramine, and not to other biogenic amines.
source: A number of receptors responding to Tyramine have been identified in Drosophila (Ohta and Ozoe, 2014; El-Kholy et al., 2015), yet only one – the GPCR TyrR – has been shown to respond specifically to Tyramine, and not to other biogenic amines (Cazzamali et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Decondensation of both Imp and Me31B was significantly impaired upon TyrR inactivation.
source: As shown in Figure 3A–E, decondensation of both Imp and Me31B was significantly impaired upon TyrR inactivation, suggesting that TyrR is the main receptor involved.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TyrR mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: TyrR is the main receptor involved in neuronal RNP granule remodeling in response to Tyramine.
source: As shown in Figure 3A–E, decondensation of both Imp and Me31B was significantly impaired upon TyrR inactivation, suggesting that TyrR is the main receptor involved.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the TyrR mutant data.

claim: Tyramine elicited calcium transients peaking 2–8 min after exposure in MB neurons.
source: Tyramine elicited calcium transients peaking 2–8 min after exposure (Figure 3F and Videos 5 and 6), as well as a modest, but reproducible and dose-dependent, long-term increase in intracellular Ca2+ (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3F and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Tyramine induced a modest, but reproducible and dose-dependent, long-term increase in intracellular Ca2+ in MB neurons.
source: Tyramine elicited calcium transients peaking 2–8 min after exposure (Figure 3F and Videos 5 and 6), as well as a modest, but reproducible and dose-dependent, long-term increase in intracellular Ca2+ (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Inactivation of TyrR largely inhibited the main calcium peak induced by Tyramine.
source: Importantly, inactivation of TyrR largely (although not completely) inhibited the main calcium peak induced by Tyramine (Figure 3F), confirming the specificity of MB neuronal response.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data from TyrR mutants shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Inhibiting the firing of MB neurons through conditional expression of Kir 2.1 significantly suppressed Tyramine-induced Imp decondensation.
source: Consistent with this idea, inhibiting the firing of MB neurons through conditional expression of the inward-rectifying potassium channel Kir 2.1 (Paradis et al., 2001) significantly suppressed Tyramine-induced Imp decondensation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating the need for both evoked responses and GPCR-mediated signaling and suggesting the existence of TyrR-expressing neurons acting as a relay to transduce Tyramine signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Tyramine-induced RNP granule remodeling requires both evoked responses and GPCR-mediated signaling.
source: Consistent with this idea, inhibiting the firing of MB neurons through conditional expression of the inward-rectifying potassium channel Kir 2.1 (Paradis et al., 2001) significantly suppressed Tyramine-induced Imp decondensation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating the need for both evoked responses and GPCR-mediated signaling and suggesting the existence of TyrR-expressing neurons acting as a relay to transduce Tyramine signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Kir2.1 experiment data.

claim: TyrR-expressing neurons act as a relay to transduce Tyramine signaling to MB neurons.
source: Consistent with this idea, inhibiting the firing of MB neurons through conditional expression of the inward-rectifying potassium channel Kir 2.1 (Paradis et al., 2001) significantly suppressed Tyramine-induced Imp decondensation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating the need for both evoked responses and GPCR-mediated signaling and suggesting the existence of TyrR-expressing neurons acting as a relay to transduce Tyramine signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations.

claim: CamkII co-immunoprecipitated with GFP-Imp, but not with sole GFP.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, CamkII co-immunoprecipitated with GFP-Imp, but not with sole GFP.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CamkII interacted with Imp both in the presence and in the absence of RNase.
source: Furthermore, CamkII interacted with Imp both in the presence and in the absence of RNase, indicating that the Imp/CamkII interaction is RNA-independent.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with and without RNase treatment.

claim: The Imp/CamkII interaction is RNA-independent.
source: Furthermore, CamkII interacted with Imp both in the presence and in the absence of RNase, indicating that the Imp/CamkII interaction is RNA-independent.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNase treatment experiment.

claim: Both CamkII and phospho-CamkII were found diffusely localized in the cytoplasm of MB γ neurons.
source: In vivo, both CamkII and phospho-CamkII (the active form of CamkII) were found diffusely localized in the cytoplasm of MB γ neurons, similar to the soluble pool of Imp molecules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No particular enrichment of CamkII was observed in Imp-containing RNP granules.
source: No particular enrichment of CamkII was observed in Imp-containing RNP granules.
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: Conditional expression of the ala peptide significantly inhibited the decondensation of Imp molecules observed upon Tyramine treatment.
source: Conditional expression of the ala peptide significantly inhibited the decondensation of Imp molecules observed upon Tyramine treatment (Figure 4B), demonstrating that CamkII is required cell-autonomously downstream of Tyramine to promote Imp decondensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CamkII is required cell-autonomously downstream of Tyramine to promote Imp decondensation.
source: Conditional expression of the ala peptide significantly inhibited the decondensation of Imp molecules observed upon Tyramine treatment (Figure 4B), demonstrating that CamkII is required cell-autonomously downstream of Tyramine to promote Imp decondensation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ala peptide inhibition experiment.

claim: Ala-mediated inhibition of CamkII did not inhibit the partial cytoplasmic relocalization of Me31B observed in response to Tyramine.
source: Ala-mediated inhibition of CamkII, however, did not inhibit the partial cytoplasmic relocalization of Me31B observed in response to Tyramine (Figure 4C), indicating that CamkII specifically modulates the decondensation of Imp.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CamkII specifically modulates the decondensation of Imp.
source: Ala-mediated inhibition of CamkII, however, did not inhibit the partial cytoplasmic relocalization of Me31B observed in response to Tyramine (Figure 4C), indicating that CamkII specifically modulates the decondensation of Imp.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential effects of CamkII inhibition on Imp versus Me31B.

claim: Treating brains with Tyramine induced a significant increase in GFP signal intensity for the construct containing profilin 3'UTR.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, treating brains with Tyramine induced a significant increase in GFP signal intensity for the construct containing profilin 3'UTR, but not for that containing SV40 3'UTR.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tyramine treatment did not induce a significant increase in GFP expression for constructs containing SV40 3'UTR.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, treating brains with Tyramine induced a significant increase in GFP signal intensity for the construct containing profilin 3'UTR, but not for that containing SV40 3'UTR.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant increase in GFP expression was observed upon prior incubation of gfp-profilin 3'UTR-expressing brains with the translation inhibitor anisomycin.
source: Furthermore, no significant increase in GFP expression was observed upon prior incubation of gfp-profilin 3'UTR-expressing brains with the translation inhibitor anisomycin (Figure 5B), indicating that increased GFP levels result from increased protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increased GFP levels from profilin 3'UTR reporters result from increased protein synthesis.
source: Furthermore, no significant increase in GFP expression was observed upon prior incubation of gfp-profilin 3'UTR-expressing brains with the translation inhibitor anisomycin (Figure 5B), indicating that increased GFP levels result from increased protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the anisomycin inhibition experiment.

claim: Increased expression of gfp-cofilin 3'UTR, but not of gfp-camk2 3'UTR reporters, was observed upon Tyramine treatment.
source: Remarkably, increased expression of gfp-cofilin 3'UTR, but not of gfp-camk2 3'UTR reporters, was observed upon Tyramine treatment (Figure 5A), suggesting that translation activation is specific to granule-associated mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Translation activation is specific to granule-associated mRNAs.
source: Remarkably, increased expression of gfp-cofilin 3'UTR, but not of gfp-camk2 3'UTR reporters, was observed upon Tyramine treatment (Figure 5A), suggesting that translation activation is specific to granule-associated mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the differential reporter responses.

claim: Blocking Imp decondensation through inhibition of CamkII prevented the translational de-repression of profilin 3'UTR reporters.
source: Further consistent with a model where RNP granule remodeling relieves associated mRNAs from translational repression, blocking Imp decondensation through inhibition of CamkII prevented the translational de-repression of profilin 3'UTR reporters (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tyramine induced within minutes the formation of bright GFP-positive cytoplasmic foci in cells expressing SunTag-tagged profilin transcripts.
source: Strikingly, Tyramine induced within minutes the formation of bright GFP-positive cytoplasmic foci (Figure 6A and Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by SunTag imaging data shown in Figure 6A and Video 7.

claim: GFP-positive cytoplasmic foci were not observed in the absence of SunTag-tagged transcripts.
source: These foci were not observed in the absence of SunTag-tagged transcripts (Figure 6A,B and Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 6A,B and Video 8.

claim: Formation of GFP-positive cytoplasmic foci was inhibited by puromycin.
source: Furthermore, their formation was inhibited by puromycin (Figure 6A,B and Video 9), indicating that they form through translation and likely correspond to translation foci.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B and Video 9.

claim: GFP-positive cytoplasmic foci form through translation and likely correspond to translation foci.
source: Furthermore, their formation was inhibited by puromycin (Figure 6A,B and Video 9), indicating that they form through translation and likely correspond to translation foci.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the puromycin inhibition experiment.

claim: The number of cells exhibiting SunTag foci peaked 2–8 min after Tyramine exposure.
source: As shown in Figure 6C and Video 7, indeed, the number of cells exhibiting SunTag foci peaked 2–8 min after Tyramine exposure, before progressively reverting to baseline values.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Activation of profilin translation occurred as a burst, with kinetics very similar to that of Tyramine-induced calcium transients.
source: Remarkably, activation of profilin translation occurred as a burst, with kinetics very similar to that of Tyramine-induced calcium transients.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of temporal profiles from different experiments.

claim: A significant decrease in the number of profilin mRNA contained in RNP granules was observed 10 min after Tyramine treatment.
source: Both experiments revealed a significant decrease in the number of profilin mRNA or reporter RNA contained in RNP granules, indicating that release of mRNAs represents an early step of granule remodeling that temporally matches with translation activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5D.

claim: Release of mRNAs represents an early step of granule remodeling that temporally matches with translation activation.
source: Both experiments revealed a significant decrease in the number of profilin mRNA or reporter RNA contained in RNP granules, indicating that release of mRNAs represents an early step of granule remodeling that temporally matches with translation activation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temporal correlation of mRNA release and translation activation.

claim: Me31B behaves as a scaffold in neuronal RNP granules.
source: These results, together with our observation that inactivation of me31B, but not of imp, prevents granule assembly (K. Pushpalatha and F. Besse, unpublished) are consistent with a model in which Me31B behaves as a scaffold, and Imp as a client whose partitioning into granules depends on Me31B, and is specifically modulated by Tyramine.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple observations including unpublished data.

claim: Imp behaves as a client whose partitioning into granules depends on Me31B.
source: These results, together with our observation that inactivation of me31B, but not of imp, prevents granule assembly (K. Pushpalatha and F. Besse, unpublished) are consistent with a model in which Me31B behaves as a scaffold, and Imp as a client whose partitioning into granules depends on Me31B, and is specifically modulated by Tyramine.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple observations including unpublished data.

claim: Translation activation and granule component decondensation exhibit distinct temporal profiles.
source: As further revealed by our real-time imaging experiments, translation activation and granule component decondensation, although both starting within minutes after Tyramine exposure, exhibit distinct temporal profiles.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of temporal data from different experiments.

claim: Translation activation occurs as a burst.
source: While translation activation occurs as a burst, decondensation of RNP components is a continuous and progressive process.
evidence: This claim is based on temporal analysis of translation data.

claim: Decondensation of RNP components is a continuous and progressive process.
source: While translation activation occurs as a burst, decondensation of RNP components is a continuous and progressive process.
evidence: This claim is based on temporal analysis of RNP component data.

claim: 51 proteins were reproducibly identified as Imp interactors by mass spectrometry analysis.
source: In total, 51 proteins were reproducibly identified, distributed into various functional categories (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: RBPs were strongly enriched in the Imp-bound fraction (22/51 proteins; p<0.001).
source: As expected, RBPs were strongly enriched in the bound fraction (22/51 proteins; p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither TyrR nor any of the other Tyramine receptors is significantly expressed in MB neurons according to single-cell transcriptomic analyses.
source: As indicated by single-cell transcriptomic analyses, neither TyrR nor any of the other Tyramine receptors is significantly expressed in MB neurons (Davie et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to single-cell transcriptomic data.

claim: Tyramine may act on MB neurons indirectly, through TyrR-expressing neurons innervating MBs.
source: Our results, however, have shown that both the calcium response and the remodeling of neuronal RNP granules triggered in MB neurons by Tyramine depend on the function of TyrR. This thus suggests that Tyramine may act on MB neurons indirectly, through TyrR-expressing neurons innervating MBs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Tyramine was shown to regulate the avoidance behavior of flies exposed to repulsive olfactory cues.
source: Potentially relevant to the known functions of MB neurons, Tyramine was in particular shown to regulate the avoidance behavior of flies exposed to repulsive olfactory cues (Kutsukake et al., 2000) and to dampen male courtship drive (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tyramine dampens male courtship drive.
source: Potentially relevant to the known functions of MB neurons, Tyramine was in particular shown to regulate the avoidance behavior of flies exposed to repulsive olfactory cues (Kutsukake et al., 2000) and to dampen male courtship drive (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.
